info.bio: The Mar-Keys, formed in 1958, was a studio session band for the Stax label that also recorded some influential hits on their own. Their backing music, along with Booker T. & the MG's, formed the foundation for the early 60s Stax sound, with their funky brand of soul music inspiring many other artists. Their organ and saxophone fuled singles released on their own led to a #3 national hit with "Last Night" in 1961. Keyboards on said track was notably played by Jerry Lee "Smoochy" Smith.

scenes.name: Soul sureño: Stax, Atlantic y FAME
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Stax era un negocio familiar en un viejo cine de Memphis, de dueños blancos (Jim Stewart y Estelle Axton) con una banda de estudio integrada (Steve Cropper, Isaac Hayes, Al Jackson, Duck Dunn, Booker T.) y solo artistas negros: ritmo pesado y vientos ásperos. Jerry Wexler llevó allí a Wilson Pickett, bailó el Jerk para enseñar el contratiempo de «In the Midnight Hour» y, cuando Stax lo vetó, lo llevó a los FAME de Rick Hall en Muscle Shoals, donde acababan de grabar «When a Man Loves a Woman» de Percy Sledge. Con una banda casi toda blanca (Spooner Oldham, Roger Hawkins) y pastillas, Pickett convirtió un estándar de cuatro años en la versión definitiva de «Land of 1000 Dances» (julio de 1966): gritos afinados, ritmo frenético, el «na, na-ne-na-na», un fragmento de un show que podría durar horas; parte de un continuo de la cultura negra entre el orgullo y la rabia. Otis Redding, heredero de Sam Cooke tras su asesinato, rompió con «I’ve Been Loving You Too Long» y Otis Blue fijó la palabra «soul», pero Stax no vendía como Motown hasta que Sam & Dave triunfaron con «Hold On! I’m Comin’». Los Beatles quisieron grabar en Stax en abril de 1966; su sonido está por todo Rubber Soul. La revista de Stax en Watts coincidió con los disturbios de agosto de 1965.

podcast.title: Developing a Distinctive Sound
podcast.body: The Mar-Keys were credited with helping Satellite Records develop the distinctive sound the label was seeking. "It was the marquees, who finally gave satellite the distinctive sound they were looking for"

podcast.title: Name Change from The Royal Spades
podcast.body: The group, originally known as The Royal Spades, was renamed The Mar-Keys by Estelle Axton, who found their original name "inappropriate." The new name was a combination of "marquee" (as in the noble title) and "keys" (as in keyboards). "Upon our marquee, as in the noble title, and keys as in keyboards, as Estelle Axton thought, entirely correctly, that their original name was inappropriate."

podcast.title: Recording Second Single Without Them
podcast.body: While The Mar-Keys were on tour, Stax studio musicians recorded the group's second single without their involvement. The band members only discovered its release when they saw it in the record shop. "The second marquee's single was recorded by the studio musicians while the group were out on tour. The first they even knew about it was when they saw it in the shop."

podcast.title: Touring Resentment
podcast.body: The Mar-Keys' tour to promote "Last Night" caused significant resentment among the black session players who had contributed to the record. These players felt the instrumental was primarily their work but that "a bunch of white boys were" receiving all the recognition. "which brought resentment from the Black Session players, some of whom claimed that during the session it hadn't even been intended as a marquee's record, and who have annoyed that even though the record was primarily their work, they weren't getting the recognition, and a bunch of white boys were."
